title: What Claude Code is
plain: Claude Code is a program that works in your project folder. It reads files, edits them, and runs commands to finish a task you describe. You can watch, correct, and review the result.
check: You type 'fix the failing test' and press Enter. What do you expect Claude Code to do first, and why does it not start editing at once?
rubric: Names the three phases: gather context (read files, run the test), take action (edit files), verify (run the test again)
Says Claude may repeat the phases several times before it stops
Names one way to take control: press Esc, type a correction, or refuse a permission prompt
try: Open a terminal in a small project and run `claude`. In the Desktop app, open the Code tab and choose the folder instead. Type: what does this project do? Claude Code shows short lines that name the files it reads, then answers. No file changes. Type /exit to leave. Optional: /powerup opens short interactive lessons.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Claude Code is a chat window that gives you text to copy into your files. Correct: it works directly in your folder, so it edits real files and runs real commands, which is why permission prompts and save points matter.

title: Where Claude Code runs
plain: Claude Code runs in a terminal, in the Desktop app's Code tab, inside VS Code or JetBrains editors, and on the web. They share one engine, but features, controls and shortcuts differ.
check: A video says 'press Shift+Tab to change the mode', but you use the Desktop app. What do you do instead, and why does the video not match your screen?
rubric: Names the place correctly: terminal, Desktop Code tab, VS Code or JetBrains, or web
Finds the mode control there: the line under the prompt (terminal), the selector next to the send button (Desktop), the mode indicator (VS Code), or the dropdown (web)
Says that a web (cloud) session works on a cloud copy of the repository, while a local session uses a folder on this computer
try: Name the place you use right now: a terminal window, the Desktop app's Code tab, a Claude Code panel inside VS Code, or claude.ai/code in a browser. Then find the control that shows the permission mode. Terminal: the line under the prompt. Desktop: the selector next to the send button. VS Code: the mode indicator at the bottom of the prompt box. Web: the dropdown next to the prompt box. Do not change it yet.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a tip from a video works the same in every place you run Claude Code. Correct: Shift+Tab belongs to the terminal version, Desktop and VS Code use a mode selector, and a web session works on a cloud copy of your repository, not on the folder on your computer.

title: Install and log in
plain: Claude Code needs a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise), a Console account, or a supported cloud provider. You install it once, then sign in. The free Claude plan is not enough.
check: You installed Claude Code, but typing `claude` in a terminal prints that the command is not found. What do you check first, and once it starts, what do you need to sign in?
rubric: Opens a new terminal window and runs claude --version; a working install prints a version number followed by (Claude Code)
Checks that the install line matched the terminal (a PowerShell prompt starts with PS; CMD does not) or follows the PATH fix on the official installation troubleshooting page
Says that signing in needs a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise) or a Console account, and that the free claude.ai plan is not enough
try: In a terminal, run `claude --version`. It prints a version number followed by (Claude Code), for example `2.1.288 (Claude Code)`. Then run `claude doctor`: it prints a read-only check of your installation and settings and does not start a session. Inside Claude Code, /doctor runs a setup checkup that can suggest fixes. If the terminal says the command is not found, open a new terminal window and try again.
pitfall: Wrong belief: any terminal accepts the install line. Correct: the line must match the terminal. On Windows, the irm line is for PowerShell (its prompt starts with PS) and the curl line with && in it is for CMD; pasting one into the other fails with an error.

title: Start in project root
plain: Claude Code works in the folder where you start it. Start it in your project's top folder, because it reads the project's .claude/settings.json (settings and hooks) only from the folder where you start.
check: You start Claude Code inside the src subfolder of your project, and the rules in the project's .claude/settings.json seem to do nothing. Why, and what do you do?
rubric: Shows the current folder with pwd and the project's top folder with git rev-parse --show-toplevel, and both name the same folder
Starts claude from that folder, not from a subfolder, the home folder, or a drive root
Runs /context and finds the project's CLAUDE.md under Memory files, or says the project has none yet
try: In your project folder run `pwd` (in CMD, run `cd` with no arguments instead), then `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` (needs Git installed). If both print the same folder, you are at the project root; one may show backslashes and the other slashes. If git says 'not a git repository', the project has no repository yet, which is fine for now. Then start `claude` from that folder.
pitfall: Wrong belief: any folder works, because Claude Code finds the project anyway. Correct: it reads .claude/settings.json, which holds hooks, only from the folder where you start it (CLAUDE.md files are also collected from the folders above), and starting in your home folder gives it access to far more than one project.

title: Folder trust dialog
plain: Starting Claude Code in a new folder shows a trust dialog. Saying yes lets that folder's own settings take effect, such as rules that pre-approve actions and hooks (commands that run automatically).
check: A friend sends you a project folder, and Claude Code shows the trust dialog on first start. What could accepting switch on, and what do you look at before you accept?
rubric: Opens .claude/settings.json (if it exists) before accepting, and looks for a hooks section and allow rules
Says that hooks run commands on your computer automatically
Knows that in a normal interactive session hooks from settings files wait until the dialog is accepted
try: Before you open a downloaded or cloned project in Claude Code, go into the project folder and list its .claude folder: run `ls .claude` (PowerShell, macOS, Linux, Git Bash) or `dir .claude` (CMD). If settings.json is there, open it in a text editor and look for the word hooks. A folder you made yourself may have no .claude folder yet; the command then reports that the path does not exist, which is normal.
pitfall: Wrong belief: the trust dialog is only a screen to click through, so accepting is always safe. Correct: accepting lets the folder's own settings run commands on your computer, so accept only for folders you made or trust; in your home folder it asks again at every start.

title: Permission prompts
plain: A permission prompt appears when Claude Code wants to do something that needs your approval, like running a command or editing a file. It shows the action. You answer Yes or No.
check: Claude Code asks permission to run `rm -r old-notes` in your project. What do you check before you answer, and what would make you say No?
rubric: Says which command or file the prompt is about and what it will change
Says whether the change can be undone, for example because it is committed in git
Chooses Yes, No, or a 'don't ask again' option on purpose and gives a reason
try: In a new practice folder, start `claude --permission-mode manual` (Desktop: choose Manual in the mode selector). The usual starting mode, Auto, asks far less often, so use Manual to see prompts. Type: create a file called hello.txt that contains the word hello. Read the prompt before you answer: it names the file and shows what will be written. Choose No once; Claude stops and waits. Ask again and choose Yes; hello.txt now exists. Delete it afterwards. If a trust dialog appears for the new folder, accept it only because you created the folder yourself a moment ago.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a permission prompt is a formality, so a quick Yes is fine. Correct: Yes lets Claude act on your computer, and 'Yes, and don't ask again' for a command saves a rule in .claude/settings.local.json that applies to later sessions too.

title: Permission modes
plain: A permission mode sets what Claude Code may do without asking. Modes: Manual, Accept edits, Plan, Auto, Don't ask, Bypass. Since version 2.1.283, terminal and VS Code sessions start in Auto when available.
check: The line under your prompt says `auto mode on`. Who decides now whether a shell command may run, and which key takes that decision back to you?
rubric: Says that in Auto a second model, the classifier, reviews the actions instead of the learner
Names Shift+Tab (Alt+M on some Windows terminals) as the terminal key, where the first press from Auto goes to Manual, or the mode selector next to the send button in Desktop

Contrasts the other modes: Manual asks before edits and shell commands; Accept edits allows file edits and common file commands (mkdir, touch, mv, cp, rm, sed) inside the project, but still asks before running the tests
try: In a practice folder run `claude` and look under the prompt for the mode text, such as `auto mode on`. Press Shift+Tab once (Alt+M on some Windows terminals). From Auto the next mode is `manual mode on`; keep pressing to see `accept edits on` and `plan mode on`, then Auto again. If you start in another mode, the order is still Manual, Accept edits, Plan, then Auto when it is available. Desktop: use the mode selector next to the send button; it remembers your choice for each folder, except Plan.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Claude Code always asks first, because Manual is the default mode. Correct: since version 2.1.283 terminal and VS Code sessions start in Auto when it is available, where a second model reviews actions instead of you, so read the mode on your screen before you start; a project's own settings file cannot switch you into Auto or Bypass.

title: Plan mode
plain: In plan mode, Claude Code reads your project and writes a plan, but does not change your project's files. You read the plan and approve it before any change starts.
check: Claude finishes a plan in plan mode and asks how to proceed. What changes the moment you approve, and what do you do before you approve?
rubric: Enters plan mode with /plan or Shift+Tab and sees plan mode on in the status bar
Says the plan back in one sentence, in their own words
Chooses an approve option or 'No, keep planning' on purpose and says what changes after approval
try: In a practice folder start `claude` and type: /plan add a file called plan-test.txt with one sentence about cats. Claude explores and shows a plan, and no file appears yet. Choose 'No, keep planning', then look in the folder: plan-test.txt does not exist. Press Shift+Tab to leave plan mode. Desktop: choose Plan in the mode selector.
pitfall: Wrong belief: plan mode is a list to approve without reading it. Correct: the plan shows what Claude will change before any file changes, so read it first; approving it ends plan mode and Claude starts editing at once. For a change you can describe in one sentence, skip plan mode.

title: Context window
plain: The context window is everything Claude can see in one session: your messages, files it read, command output, and CLAUDE.md. It has a size limit, and results get worse as more of it is used.
check: After three hours in one session, Claude starts ignoring a rule you typed in your first message. What probably happened, and where should that rule live so it survives?
rubric: Names the filling context window, or a compaction that summarized the early message, as the likely cause
Looks at what uses the space with /context (Desktop: the usage ring next to the model picker)
Moves the rule into CLAUDE.md, or starts fresh with /clear and a clearer first prompt
try: In a session where Claude has already read a few files, type `/context`. You see a colored grid that shows how full the window is, a breakdown by category, and a list called Memory files that names the CLAUDE.md files that loaded. Nothing changes; it only reports. Desktop: click the usage ring next to the model picker.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Claude remembers everything said in a long chat equally well, so longer is better. Correct: the window has a limit and every file and output uses part of it, so old details get dropped or summarized; start a new conversation with /clear for unrelated tasks and keep lasting rules in CLAUDE.md.

title: Start fresh with /clear
plain: /clear starts a new, empty conversation. Claude forgets what was said before, but your files and the old conversation stay on disk: reopen the old one with /resume.
check: You are in the middle of a project and run /clear. What is gone, what is still there, and how can you get the old conversation back?
rubric: Types /clear (or its aliases /reset or /new) when switching to an unrelated task
Shows that Claude has no memory of the earlier messages by asking about them
Finds the old conversation again with /resume and presses Esc to close the list
try: In a practice folder start `claude` and send: Reply with only the word banana. Then type `/clear`. Now ask: What word did I ask you to reply with earlier? Claude cannot know, because the conversation is empty. Type `/resume`, find the earlier conversation in the list, and press Esc to close the list.
pitfall: Wrong belief: /clear undoes Claude's work. Correct: it only empties the conversation; files Claude edited stay edited, and to undo file edits you use /rewind or git.

title: Compacting a long chat
plain: Compacting replaces a long conversation with a short summary to free space. Claude Code does it automatically near the limit, or when you type /compact. Details from early messages can be lost.
check: You told Claude in chat 'always run the tests before you say you are done', and after /compact it stops doing so. Why, and what is the fix?
rubric: The project-root CLAUDE.md survives: it is read again from disk
A rule given only in chat may be lost or only summarized, so it belongs in CLAUDE.md
Exact command output is replaced by the summary
try: In a session that already has some back-and-forth, for example after you asked Claude to explain two files, run `/context`, then `/compact focus on the file names`, then `/context` again. A 'Conversation compacted' message appears and the usage is usually lower. Your files do not change.
pitfall: Wrong belief: compaction keeps the whole conversation in a smaller size. Correct: it keeps a summary, so exact wording and long outputs are gone; decisions that must last belong in CLAUDE.md or in a file.

title: Resume a session
plain: Claude Code saves each conversation on your computer, linked to the folder you worked in. In that folder, `claude --continue` reopens the latest one; `claude --resume` or `/resume` lets you pick an older one.
check: You worked on a project on Friday. On Monday you open a terminal in another folder, run `claude --continue`, and see 'No conversation found to continue'. Why, and how do you fix it?
rubric: Goes back to the project's folder (cd) and runs claude --continue there, because --continue looks only at the current folder
Sees the earlier messages again and continues the work
Opens the list with claude --resume or /resume and chooses an older or named conversation
try: Type `/exit`, then run `claude --continue` in the same folder: the last conversation reopens with its earlier messages. Try `/rename my-first-chat`, leave with /exit, and run `claude --resume my-first-chat` to open it by name. Desktop: click the session in the sidebar.
pitfall: Wrong belief: typing `claude` again continues my last conversation, or closing the window deletes it. Correct: `claude` alone starts a new, empty conversation; the old one stays saved on your computer (30 days by default) and comes back with `claude --continue` or `/resume`.

title: Undo with /rewind
plain: Claude Code takes a checkpoint before each prompt. /rewind (or Esc twice) restores code, conversation, or both to an earlier prompt. It tracks only Claude's file-edit tools, so it does not replace git.
check: Claude ran a shell command that deleted notes.txt, and now you open /rewind. What do you expect for notes.txt, and what should you have done before that turn?
rubric: The edit-tool change can be restored
The rm change is not tracked, so git is the way back
Your own edits outside Claude are normally not tracked
try: In a practice folder start `claude` and ask: create notes.txt with the line first. Then ask: add a second line to notes.txt that says second. Type `/rewind` (or press Esc twice on an empty prompt), pick the second prompt, and choose Restore code. Open notes.txt: it has one line again, and the conversation is still there. This works because Claude edits files with its file tools; a change made by a shell command is not restored. VS Code: hover over a message and use the rewind button.
pitfall: Wrong belief: /rewind is a full undo for everything Claude does. Correct: it covers only Claude's file-edit tools; shell commands (rm, mv, cp), most subagent edits, and changes you make yourself are not restored, so commit to git before a big change.

title: CLAUDE.md file
plain: CLAUDE.md is a text file of instructions that Claude Code reads at the start of every session. Put project facts and rules there, such as how to run tests. Keep it short.
check: Your CLAUDE.md says 'be careful with files' and Claude still overwrote one. How would you change the instruction so that it can be followed?
rubric: Creates the file at ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md (both load; ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is for all your projects), by hand or with /init, with checkable lines such as the test command
Starts a new session and finds the file under Memory files in /context
Rewrites a vague line such as 'format code nicely' into a specific one
try: In a practice folder start `claude` and ask: create a file CLAUDE.md in this folder with one line: Start every answer with the word Noted. Approve the write if asked. Type /exit and start `claude` again in the same folder. Run `/context` and look for CLAUDE.md under Memory files. Ask: what is 2 plus 2? The answer usually starts with Noted. Delete CLAUDE.md afterwards if you do not want it.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a rule in CLAUDE.md is always obeyed, and a longer file is better. Correct: Claude reads it as context, not as an enforced setting, so short and specific lines (under about 200) work best, and anything that must happen every time belongs in a hook or a permission rule.

title: Auto memory
plain: Auto memory is notes Claude Code writes for itself, such as your preferences and corrections. They are plain files on your computer, and the first part is read at each session start.
check: You told Claude 'always use pnpm' last week, and in a new session today it still knows. Where does that knowledge live, and how would you look at it or delete it?
rubric: Runs /memory and finds the auto memory switch and the option that opens its folder
Reads MEMORY.md or one note and names its kind (user, feedback, project or reference), or confirms that nothing is saved yet
Says that the notes are stored on this computer, not in the project, and can be edited or deleted
try: In a session run `/memory`. You see your CLAUDE.md files, a switch for auto memory, and an option that opens the auto memory folder (in ~/.claude/projects/, one folder per project). Open the folder and read MEMORY.md if it exists. Do not change anything.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Claude automatically remembers everything we say, and auto memory is the same as CLAUDE.md. Correct: Claude saves only what it judges useful later, you write CLAUDE.md while Claude writes auto memory, and both are plain files you can read, edit or delete; auto memory stays on your computer and is not shared with teammates.
